q: How to tell if a photo is AI generated
title: How to tell if a photo is AI generated
description: No single check proves a photo is real or AI. Here are the checks that work today: source, credentials, reverse search, and what to look for.
short: No single check proves a photo is real or AI generated. Combine four: find where the photo came from, look for Content Credentials, run a reverse image search, and inspect the details. Visual tells like odd hands fade as tools improve, so the source matters more than the pixels.

sections.h: Start with where the photo came from
sections.html:
The most reliable question is not "does this look fake" but "who shared this first, and can I reach them?" A photographer, an outlet or a person at the event can usually say where and when it was taken. A screenshot with no name and no link gives you nothing to check.

Look at the account that posted it. A long history of original work is a good sign. A new account posting dramatic images with no other content is a reason to slow down.

Content Credentials (the C2PA standard) are a signed record attached to a file that can show who made it, with what tool, and what was edited. Drop the file into the Content Credentials Verify tool (the old address contentcredentials.org/verify forwards there) to read it.

Two honest limits. First, many photos have no credentials at all, and that does not make them fake. Second, credentials can be lost when a file is re-saved, screenshotted or re-encoded by a platform. A missing record is silence, not a verdict.

Upload the image or paste its link into Google search by image (in Chrome, right-click and choose Search with Google Lens) or into TinEye. You are looking for an earlier copy, a caption that contradicts the claim, or the original photographer. If a "breaking" photo shows up years old, you have your answer.

A brand-new image will return nothing, so an empty result proves nothing either way.

sections.h: Look closely at the image itself
sections.html:
Zoom in. Common tells include text that is almost-letters, hands or teeth that do not add up, jewelry or glasses that merge into skin, shadows that point in different directions, repeated patterns in crowds and backgrounds that melt together. Treat these as hints. Newer tools get many of them right, and real photos can show odd artifacts from compression or editing.

Also ask whether the scene makes sense: weather, signs, uniforms and landmarks can often be checked against other photos from the same place and day.

Every post on Emera carries a signed record (C2PA content credentials) of who shared it and when it went up. A Signed badge says exactly what was checked and nothing more. Reposts point back to the original post, so you can follow a picture to the person who first shared it. Emera does not detect AI images and does not tell you a photo is real; it shows you what was recorded so you can judge.

faqs.q: Can an AI detector tell me for sure?
faqs.a: No. Detector tools give probabilities, make mistakes in both directions and fall behind new image generators. Use them as one input next to the source and a reverse image search.

faqs.q: Does a missing Content Credential mean the photo is fake?
faqs.a: No. Most photos online carry no credentials, and platforms or screenshots can strip them. Absence is not evidence either way.

faqs.q: Does a present Content Credential mean the photo is true?
faqs.a: No. It records who signed the file and what was done to it. It does not say the scene is accurate or that the caption is honest.

faqs.q: What is the fastest check?
faqs.a: A reverse image search. It takes under a minute and often finds the original or an earlier copy.

q: How to tell if a video is real or fake
title: How to tell if a video is real or fake
description: No one check proves a video is real. Fact-checker steps for news clips, event footage and deepfakes: source, keyframe search, context, credentials.
short: No single check proves a video is real or fake. Fact-checkers trace it: find the earliest upload, pull still frames and reverse search them, check that place, date and weather match the claim, and look for Content Credentials. A clip with no earlier copy is not proven new or authentic.

sections.html: Most misleading videos are real footage with a false caption, often an old clip from another event. Search the claim, the location and key phrases on several platforms and sort by oldest. Fact-checkers report finding clips that predate the event they supposedly show by days or years.

sections.h: Search by keyframes, not the whole video
sections.html:
Reverse search works on images, so pull still frames from the video and search each one. The free InVID-WeVerify plugin extracts keyframes and sends them to Google, Bing, Yandex and TinEye. Full Fact's guide suggests trying more than one engine, since results differ.

Searching in other languages can surface debunks an English search misses. And a brand-new video will return nothing, which does not prove it is genuine.

sections.h: Check that the scene fits the claim
sections.html: Compare what you can see with what is claimed: signs and language, vehicles, uniforms, shop fronts, skyline, weather, shadows and time of day. Match them against maps and other footage from that place and date. For news events, check whether established outlets or local reporters have published the same footage and where they got it.

sections.h: Watch for edits and synthetic video
sections.html:
Deepfakes and fully generated clips can show lip movement that drifts from the audio, flickering around the face or hairline, objects that change shape between frames and hands or text that warp. These tells are getting rarer. Cuts that remove context matter just as much: ask what happened before and after the clip.

Metadata can help but is not reliable, since it is often stripped on upload and can be edited.

If the file carries Content Credentials, the Verify tool shows who signed it and what tool made or edited it. Many videos have none, and platforms can remove them, so treat them as a bonus when present, not a requirement.

Every post on Emera carries a signed record (C2PA content credentials) of who shared it and when it went up. A Signed badge says exactly what was checked and nothing more. Reposts point back to the original post, so you can see who shared a clip first. Emera does not fact-check videos or promise that anything is real.

faqs.q: Can I trust a video because many people shared it?
faqs.a: No. Sharing counts say how popular a clip is, not whether it is genuine. Many viral clips are old footage with new captions.

faqs.q: How do I spot a deepfake?
faqs.a: Check the source first, then look for mismatched lip movement, flicker near the face, warped hands or text and odd lighting. None of these is conclusive, and good fakes avoid them.

faqs.q: What if my reverse search finds nothing?
faqs.a: That means no earlier copy was indexed, not that the video is real. Keep checking the source, location and other reporting.

faqs.q: Is there a tool that gives a yes or no?
faqs.a: Not one you should rely on. Detection tools give estimates and are wrong in both directions.

q: How to prevent people from stealing your art online
title: How to prevent people from stealing your art online
description: You cannot stop all copying, but you can make theft harder and easier to prove: sizes, credits, records, registration, and protection tools.
short: You cannot fully prevent copying once art is public, but you can make theft harder and easier to prove. Post smaller files, keep dated originals, put your name in the file, register important work with your copyright office, and know the takedown route before you need it.

sections.h: Make the original easy to prove
sections.html:
In a dispute, the person who can show the work in progress usually wins. Keep layered files, sketches, raw photos and exports with their dates. Post a lower-resolution version publicly and keep the full-resolution file to yourself.

Put your name in the file's metadata and, if it suits the piece, a small mark in a corner. A mark that sits across the image is harder to crop out than one in a corner but changes how the work looks, so it is your call.

In the United States, registration is generally required before you can sue for infringement (17 U.S.C. 411), and statutory damages and attorney's fees are generally unavailable for infringement that began before registration unless an exception applies, such as registering within three months of first publication (17 U.S.C. 412). Rules differ in other countries and this is not legal advice. Confirm the details with your copyright office.

sections.h: Consider protection tools, with honest limits
sections.html: Glaze and Nightshade, from the University of Chicago's SAND Lab, add changes to images meant to disrupt how AI models learn an artist's style. Researchers and reviewers note limits: the changes can be visible on flat-color art, they are not future-proof, and they do nothing to stop a person from reposting your file. Confirm current details on the project page.

sections.h: Know where your work shows up
sections.html: Run a reverse image search on your best-known pieces every so often, using Google search by image or TinEye. Early discovery makes a takedown simpler. If you find a copy, see what to do if someone steals your artwork.

Every post on Emera carries a signed record (C2PA content credentials) of who shared it and when it went up. A Signed badge says exactly what was checked and nothing more. Reposts point back to the original post. Upload once and Emera scans the web for copies, files the takedown on whatever platform they turn up, and when a takedown is not enough, its agents take the legal steps with you. Found one yourself? Report it from any post, and every step shows on your dashboard.

faqs.q: Does a watermark stop theft?
faqs.a: No. It makes casual reposting less appealing and helps you prove origin, but a determined person can crop or edit it out.

faqs.q: Is right-click protection worth it?
faqs.a: No. Anything shown on a screen can be saved, so it only annoys honest visitors.

faqs.q: Do I need to register my art?
faqs.a: Not to own it, but in the US registration is generally needed before you can sue, and timing affects damages. Check your own country's rules.

faqs.q: Will Glaze or Nightshade stop all AI training?
faqs.a: No. They are described by their makers and independent reviewers as a partial measure that may weaken over time.

q: What to do if someone steals your artwork
title: What to do if someone steals your artwork
description: Step by step if your art was copied: gather proof, contact the person, file a takedown with the platform, and when to talk to a lawyer.
short: Save proof first: links, screenshots with dates and your original files. Then message the poster, and if that fails file a takedown with the platform's copyright form. A US-style takedown notice has six required parts. For money or repeat copying, talk to a copyright lawyer.

sections.h: Step 1: collect proof before anything changes
sections.html:
1. Copy the exact link to each copy and the account that posted it.
  2. Take screenshots that show the date, the account name and the caption.
  3. Collect your originals: layered files, sketches, raw exports and your first post of the work with its date.
  4. Note any profit being made from it, such as a shop listing or an ad.

sections.h: Step 2: decide whether to contact the person first
sections.html: A short, calm message often works when the copy looks like a fan repost or a mistake. Say it is your work, link your original and ask them to remove it or credit you. Skip this step if the account is a business copying at scale or you expect hostility. Going straight to the platform is fine.

sections.h: Step 3: file a takedown with the platform
sections.html:
Most large platforms have a copyright form. A notice under U.S. law has to include six things: a signature, the work you own, the material you want removed with enough detail to find it, your contact details, a statement of good-faith belief that the use is not authorized, and a statement that your information is accurate and, under penalty of perjury, that you are the owner or authorized to act for them (17 U.S.C. 512(c)(3)). For Instagram specifically, see how to file a DMCA takedown on Instagram.

Only file if you are sure. Knowingly misrepresenting that material is infringing can make you liable for damages (section 512(f)).

The person who posted can file a counter-notification. If a valid one arrives, the platform forwards it to you and must restore the material 10 to 14 business days later unless you tell it you have filed a court action (section 512(g)). Decide beforehand whether you would go to court.

sections.h: Step 5: know when to bring in a lawyer
sections.html: Consider one if someone is selling your work, repeats the copying or ignores notices. In the US, registration is generally needed before suing, so register early for pieces that matter. This page is general information, not legal advice.

Upload once and Emera scans the web for copies, files the takedown on whatever platform they turn up, and when a takedown is not enough, its agents take the legal steps with you. Found one yourself? Report it from any post, and every step shows on your dashboard.

faqs.q: Can I just report the post inside the app?
faqs.a: For copyright, use the platform's dedicated copyright form. General reporting menus often route to other policies. On Instagram, use the Copyright Report Form.

faqs.q: Do I need to register my art before sending a takedown?
faqs.a: A takedown notice does not require registration. Suing for infringement in the US generally does.

faqs.q: What if they credited me?
faqs.a: Credit is not permission. You can still ask for removal or a license, though a friendly message may settle it faster.

faqs.q: Can I be penalized for filing?
faqs.a: If you knowingly misrepresent infringement, yes, under section 512(f). A good-faith notice from the real owner is fine.

q: How to file a DMCA takedown on Instagram
title: How to file a DMCA takedown on Instagram
description: Use Instagram's Copyright Report Form, not the in-app Report button. What to prepare, what the notice needs, and what happens after.
short: Use Instagram's Copyright Report Form in the Help Center, not the in-app Report button. You must be the rights owner or their authorized representative. Have the post links, a link to your original and your contact details ready, and only submit if the claim is accurate.

sections.html:
Instagram's Help Center says only the rights owner or an authorized representative can get a copyright report processed. Appearing in a photo or video does not by itself make you the copyright owner. Gather:

  • The exact URL of each infringing post or account
  • A link or file showing your original and its date
  • Your name, address and email

Read Instagram's page on what to consider before submitting an IP report, which also covers false reports and counter notices.

1. Open the Instagram Copyright Report Form (it opens a Meta reporting form). Confirm the wording and fields on that page, since forms change.
  2. Say you are the owner or acting for the owner.
  3. Identify your work and paste the links to the content you want removed.
  4. Describe the work and why the content infringes it.
  5. Give your contact details and sign electronically.

sections.h: What the law requires in a notice
sections.html: Under 17 U.S.C. 512(c)(3) a notice needs a signature, identification of the work, identification of the infringing material with enough detail to find it, your contact information, a good-faith statement that the use is not authorized and an accuracy statement made under penalty of perjury. Knowingly lying in a notice can make you liable for damages (section 512(f)).

Meta reviews the report and may remove the content. The uploader is told and can file a counter-notification. If a valid one arrives, the material can be restored 10 to 14 business days after it is received unless you file a court action first (section 512(g)). Meta says it may take action against accounts that submit fraudulent reports.

Do not use the three-dot Report menu for copyright; use the form.

Emera helps you file takedowns for copies of your work elsewhere. You report a copy you found, Emera helps with the paperwork, and every step shows on your dashboard. Nothing is sent until you confirm it.

faqs.q: Is a DMCA takedown the same as reporting a post?
faqs.a: No. A DMCA takedown is a formal copyright notice with legal statements. The regular Report button is for other policy violations.

faqs.q: Does it cost anything?
faqs.a: The form is free to submit. A lawyer is optional.

faqs.q: How long does removal take?
faqs.a: It varies and Instagram does not promise a time. Check the Help Center for current guidance.

faqs.q: Can I file for someone else?
faqs.a: Yes, if you are an authorized representative of the owner and say so on the form.

q: What are content credentials
title: What are Content Credentials
description: Content Credentials (C2PA) are a signed record of where a file came from and how it was edited. How to check one, and what they cannot prove.
short: Content Credentials are a signed record attached to a photo, video or file that shows where it came from and how it was edited. They follow the open C2PA standard. You can check a file at the Verify tool. They show a file's history, not whether what it shows is true.

sections.html:
Content Credentials are the name for the open standard from the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA). The C2PA site compares them to a nutrition label: a look at a file's history that anyone can read. Its steering committee includes Adobe, Amazon, BBC, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Sony, TikTok and Truepic.

A credential is a signed bundle of facts, such as who created the file, what tool made it and what edits followed, tied to the file so tampering can be noticed.

1. Go to the Content Credentials Verify tool (contentcredentials.org/verify forwards to it).
  2. Upload the original file or use a supported link.
  3. Read the result: who signed it, the tool used and the edit history, if any.

Use the original file where you can. Screenshots and files re-saved by messengers or social platforms often lose the record.

A credential records provenance. It does not say that a scene is real, that a caption is honest or that the signer is trustworthy. A missing credential does not make a file fake either: most files online have none. Treat credentials as one clue next to the source and a reverse image search.

Support is spread across cameras, editing software, AI tools and some platforms, and it keeps changing. Check the C2PA site for the current list of members and products rather than assuming a given app supports them.

Every post on Emera carries a signed record (C2PA content credentials) of who shared it and when it went up. A Signed badge says exactly what was checked and nothing more. Emera does not say a post is true or guarantee that it is real, and it does not detect AI.

faqs.q: Are Content Credentials the same as a watermark?
faqs.a: No. A watermark is a mark in the pixels. Content Credentials are signed metadata about the file's history. They can also be lost when a file is re-saved.

faqs.q: Do they stop deepfakes?
faqs.a: No. They help you check files that carry a credential. A fake with no credential is still possible, and a missing credential proves nothing.

faqs.q: Is C2PA the same thing?
faqs.a: C2PA is the standards group and technical specification. Content Credentials is the public name for the resulting record.

faqs.q: Does it cost money to check one?
faqs.a: The Verify tool is free to use.

q: Is there social media without an algorithm
title: Is there social media without an algorithm
description: Yes, partly. Chronological feeds on Instagram, Bluesky and Mastodon, plus open algorithms you choose. What each option really gives you.
short: Yes, partly. Instagram has a Following feed in time order, Bluesky's Following feed is chronological and it lets you pick custom feeds, and Mastodon has lists and a timeline of people you follow. Few services have zero ranking anywhere, so check each feed's label.

sections.html: Any list of posts has some order. The real question is who chooses it. A chronological feed orders by time. A ranked feed orders by a system's guess at what you will engage with. A choice of feeds lets you pick the ordering yourself.

Instagram offers a Following feed (posts from accounts you follow) and a Favorites feed. According to widely published guides, tap the Instagram logo at the top left of the home screen and choose Following or Favorites; the setting may not stick between sessions. Confirm the steps on Instagram's Help Center page.

Bluesky's docs describe the Following feed as the default timeline of accounts you follow, and its custom feeds let developers publish ranking methods that anyone can choose. A feed can be a chronological list or one filtered to a topic.

Mastodon's docs describe lists as subsets of your home timeline, plus live feeds of public posts your server knows about. Confirm the ordering on the Mastodon docs. Because servers are independent, features vary by host.

Time order is predictable but favors people who post often, and it can bury a post you would have wanted. Ranked feeds surface more but hide the reasoning. Following only the accounts you care about and using lists gives you control on any service.
Posts on Emera show a Why you are seeing this reason, and you can pick your feeds. Emera runs as a nonprofit and the code is open source.

faqs.q: Is a chronological feed better?
faqs.a: It is more predictable, but not always better. You may miss things when you are away because feeds fill quickly.

faqs.q: Can I turn the algorithm off on Instagram?
faqs.a: Not entirely, but the Following and Favorites feeds order posts by time. Confirm the steps on the Help Center page.

faqs.q: What is a custom feed?
faqs.a: A feed built by someone else, or by you, with its own rules, which you choose to follow. On Bluesky anyone can publish one.

faqs.q: Do any platforms have no ranking at all?
faqs.a: Few do everywhere. Search, suggestions and notifications often rank things even when your main feed does not.

q: How much can you sue for copyright infringement
title: How much can you sue for copyright infringement
description: In the US a court can award your losses plus the copier's profits, or $750 to $30,000 per work, up to $150,000 if willful. What decides which applies.
short: In the US, a court can award either your actual losses plus the copier's profits, or statutory damages of $750 to $30,000 per work, and up to $150,000 per work if the copying was willful. Statutory damages and legal fees generally depend on registering your work early. Courts set the number, so nothing here is a promise.

sections.h: Two ways the money is counted
sections.html:
US law lets a copyright owner pick one of two measures once infringement is proved (17 U.S.C. 504).

  • Actual damages and profits. What you lost because of the copying, plus the infringer's profits from it. You only have to show their gross revenue; they have to prove their costs.
  • Statutory damages. A court-set amount per work instead, from $750 to $30,000. If the copying was willful the court can go up to $150,000 per work. If the copier proves they had no reason to know it was infringing, the court can go as low as $200.

The count is per work, not per copy. One illustration copied onto fifty shirts is one work.

sections.h: Registration decides which options you have
sections.html: For a US work you generally have to register before you can sue at all (section 411). Statutory damages and attorney's fees are barred if the copying began before you registered, unless you registered within three months of first publishing the work (section 412). Unregistered work can still support a claim for actual losses and profits, which are often small for one creator. See how to register a copyright in the US.

A court may award costs and a reasonable attorney's fee to the winning side (section 505). That cuts both ways: the loser can be ordered to pay. Some lawyers take cases on contingency, which means they are paid from what is recovered.

sections.h: A cheaper route for smaller amounts
sections.html: The Copyright Claims Board is a three-member tribunal inside the US Copyright Office. Claims are capped at $30,000 total, you do not need a lawyer, and it can award statutory damages of up to $15,000 per work. Details are on copyright small claims court.

It depends on three things: whether the copier made money, whether your work was registered in time, and how many of your works were copied. A single repost with no revenue is often settled faster with a takedown. A brand or shop earning money from your work is the case where a claim letter and a lawyer make sense.

This page is general information, not legal advice. For your own case, talk to a copyright lawyer.

Emera Protect finds copies and fake accounts and files the takedowns. When someone made money from your work, Get paid sends the claim letter, and if they do not pay, partner copyright lawyers in the US take it to court. It is no win, no fee, and you keep 70% of what is recovered. Results depend on the facts of each case.

faqs.q: Is there a minimum I can claim?
faqs.a: Statutory damages start at $750 per work, and a court can go to $200 if the copier proves they did not know the use was infringing. Actual damages can be any amount you can show.

faqs.q: Do I need to register before I send a takedown?
faqs.a: No. A takedown notice does not need registration. Suing for infringement of a US work generally does.

faqs.q: Can I get statutory damages for work I registered after it was copied?
faqs.a: Generally not, unless you registered within three months of first publishing it. Section 412 bars statutory damages and attorney's fees for copying that began before registration.

faqs.q: How long do I have to bring a claim?
faqs.a: The Copyright Claims Board says three years from when the infringing activity took place. Confirm the deadline for your situation with a lawyer.

q: Statutory damages for copyright infringement: how they work
title: Statutory damages for copyright: how they work
description: Statutory damages are $750 to $30,000 per work, up to $150,000 if willful. When they apply, when they do not, and the 3 month registration rule.
short: Statutory damages are a court-set amount per work instead of proving your losses: $750 to $30,000, up to $150,000 per work if the copying was willful. They apply only if you registered the work before the copying began or within three months of first publication. Courts decide each amount.

sections.html:
Proving what a copy cost you can be hard, especially for a creator whose work was reposted for free. Statutory damages skip that step. Under 17 U.S.C. 504(c) the owner can elect, before the court's final judgment, a set sum per work "as the court considers just".

  • Standard range: $750 to $30,000 per work.
  • Willful infringement: up to $150,000 per work.
  • Innocent infringement, if the copier proves they had no reason to believe it was infringing: down to $200.

The unit is the work. A song copied into 20 videos is one work. Ten different registered photos copied by the same shop are ten works, so the range for that set is $7,500 to $300,000 before any willfulness finding. A court picks where in the range. These are limits, not forecasts.

sections.h: The registration rule that decides everything
sections.html:
Section 412 bars statutory damages and attorney's fees when copying of a published work starts after publication but before you register, unless you register within three months of first publication. For an unpublished work, the copying must start after registration.

This is why creators who register late find the big numbers off the table. The fix costs $45 to $65 per application today. See how to register a copyright in the US.

sections.h: What if you missed the window
sections.html:
You can still claim actual damages and the copier's profits, and you can still send takedowns. And registering now protects you against future copying of the same work, since statutory damages can apply to copying that begins after registration.

This page is general information, not legal advice. For your own case, talk to a copyright lawyer.

Emera Protect finds the copies and documents them, which is the proof any claim starts with. Get paid then sends a claim letter to the copier, and partner copyright lawyers in the US take it further if they do not pay. No win, no fee, and you keep 70%. We help you register your work when it can raise what a court awards.

faqs.q: What is the difference between actual and statutory damages?
faqs.a: Actual damages are your proven losses plus the copier's profits. Statutory damages are a set range per work that a court chooses without you proving a dollar loss.

faqs.q: Can I get $150,000 for one photo?
faqs.a: That is the legal ceiling for willful infringement of one registered work, not a typical award. A court decides, and most facts do not reach it.

faqs.q: Do statutory damages apply to unregistered work?
faqs.a: No. Under section 412 they depend on timely registration.

faqs.q: Does a takedown need registration?
faqs.a: No. Only suing over a US work generally does.

q: Someone stole my video: what to do
title: Someone stole my video: what to do
description: Reposted your video without asking? Save proof, use the platform's copyright form, and know when a claim for money makes sense.
short: Save the link and a dated screenshot of the copy, keep your original file, then file a copyright report on the platform where it was reposted. A direct message can work for a friendly repost. If the account is making money from your video, ask about a claim for what it earned.

sections.h: Step 1: keep proof before anything changes
sections.html:
1. Copy the exact link to the repost and the username that posted it.
  2. Screenshot it with the date, the account name, the caption and the view count.
  3. Keep your original export or raw file and the link to your first post of it, with its date.
  4. Note anything that shows income: a sponsor tag, a shop link, an ad.

sections.h: Step 2: decide whether to message first
sections.html: If it looks like a fan repost with no credit, a short note often works: "This is my video, here is the original, please take it down or credit me." Skip this if the account runs many reposts or you expect a fight. Going straight to a copyright report is always fine.

sections.h: Step 3: use the copyright form, not the general report
sections.html: Each large platform has a dedicated copyright report. Steps for the two most common: TikTok, YouTube, and for Instagram see how to file a takedown on Instagram. A notice needs a few legal parts; the template lists them.

sections.h: Step 4: check whether it is worth more than a takedown
sections.html:
If the account earned from your video, or a brand used it in an ad, you may be owed money. Registered work can reach statutory damages of $750 to $30,000 per work. Read how much you can sue for before deciding.

This page is general information, not legal advice. For your own case, talk to a copyright lawyer.

q: How to file a DMCA takedown on TikTok
title: How to file a DMCA takedown on TikTok
description: Use TikTok's copyright report form with links to the copy and your original. What the notice needs and what happens after you send it.
short: Use TikTok's copyright report form, not the regular report menu. You must own the work or act for the owner. Have the link to each copy, a link to your original and your contact details ready, and only submit a claim you are sure of. Confirm the current form fields on TikTok's page.

sections.html:
Only the rights owner or an authorized agent should file. Appearing in a video does not make you its copyright owner. Gather:

  • The link to each copy (open the video, tap share, copy link) and the username

  4. Add your contact details and sign electronically.

sections.h: What a notice has to say

Knowingly lying in a notice can make you liable for damages (section 512(f)). The template has all six.

The platform reviews it and may remove the video. The poster can file a counter-notification; if a valid one arrives, the video can be restored 10 to 14 business days later unless you tell the platform you filed a court action (section 512(g)). Decide beforehand whether you would go to court.

title: How to file a DMCA takedown on YouTube
description: File a copyright removal request in YouTube Studio under Content detection. What it asks for, what the uploader sees and what happens next.
short: In YouTube Studio open Content detection, then New removal request. You must own the content or act for the owner, give direct links to the copies, and sign two legal statements. Consider fair use first, since an insufficient answer can make the request invalid. Never submit false information.

sections.html:
1. Sign in to YouTube Studio with the account linked to your channel.
  2. Open Content detection in the left menu.
  3. Choose New removal request.
  4. Add the links to the videos you want removed and describe your original work.

YouTube's own guide also covers email, fax and mail submissions for videos and for non-video content such as channel banners.

• Contact details: an email, address or phone number.
  • A clear description of your copyrighted work, or a representative list.
  • Direct links in the format YouTube lists for each content type (watch, Shorts, playlist).

sections.h: Fair use and the 7 day option

You can also schedule the removal to take effect in 7 days, which gives the uploader time to act and may help them avoid a strike. That is a kind option for a first-time repost.

sections.h: What the uploader sees and what happens next

YouTube reviews the request for required information and apparent validity, and removes the content if it passes. If information is missing it contacts you, and the video may stay up meanwhile. Your name, primary email and the description of your work may be shared with the uploader; your physical address and phone number stay confidential unless requested for a lawsuit.

The uploader can send a counter-notification. A valid one can lead to restoration 10 to 14 business days later unless you file a court action (section 512(g)).

q: DMCA takedown notice template
title: DMCA takedown notice template (copy and paste)
description: A plain DMCA takedown notice you can copy: the six parts US law requires, a fill-in template, and what to do after you send it.
short: A DMCA takedown notice needs six parts: a signature, your work, the infringing material with its location, your contact details, a good-faith statement and an accuracy statement under penalty of perjury (17 U.S.C. 512(c)(3)). Copy the template below, fill in the brackets and send it to the platform's copyright agent or form.

sections.h: The six parts a notice needs
sections.html:
1. A physical or electronic signature of the owner or an authorized agent.
  2. Identification of the copyrighted work you say was infringed.
  3. Identification of the infringing material, with enough information for the platform to find it (links).
  4. Your contact information: address, phone, email.
  5. A statement that you have a good-faith belief the use is not authorized by the owner, its agent or the law.
  6. A statement that the information is accurate and, under penalty of perjury, that you are the owner or authorized to act (17 U.S.C. 512(c)(3)).

Subject: Copyright takedown notice

To the Copyright Agent of [platform or website]:

1. I am the owner of the copyright in [title and short description of your work], first published at [link to your original] on [date].

2. The following material infringes my copyright and is located at: [link 1], [link 2].

3. I have a good-faith belief that the use of this material is not authorized by me, my agent or the law.

4. The information in this notice is accurate, and under penalty of perjury, I am the owner of the exclusive right that is allegedly infringed, or am authorized to act on the owner's behalf.

5. My contact details: [full legal name], [address], [phone], [email].

Signed: /[full legal name]/ Date: [date]

Please remove or disable access to the material promptly.

Most large platforms prefer their own form, which collects the same parts: Instagram, TikTok, YouTube. For a website, look for a designated copyright agent on its terms page or in the US Copyright Office directory, or send the notice to its hosting company.

Only send a notice you are sure of. Knowingly misrepresenting that material is infringing can make you liable for damages (section 512(f)). Consider whether the use might be fair use. Expect a possible counter-notice, after which the material can be restored in 10 to 14 business days unless you file a court action (section 512(g)).

This page is general information, not legal advice. For your own case, talk to a copyright lawyer.

q: Copyright small claims court: how the CCB works
title: Copyright small claims court: how the CCB works
description: The Copyright Claims Board decides copyright claims up to $30,000 without a lawyer. Fees, limits, who can opt out and the 3 year deadline.
short: The Copyright Claims Board (CCB) is a US tribunal for copyright claims up to $30,000 in total, with statutory damages capped at $15,000 per work. You do not need a lawyer. It costs $40 to file and $60 more if the other side does not opt out. You need a registration or a submitted application.

sections.html: The Copyright Claims Board is a three-member tribunal in the US Copyright Office, described as a streamlined alternative to federal court. It hears copyright claims where you want money, and it is built for people without a lawyer.

• Total damages are capped at $30,000.
  • Statutory damages are capped at $15,000 per work.
  • Claims of $5,000 or less can use the Smaller Claims procedure.
  • You need a registration or an application filed before or with your claim. If the application is refused, the claim is dismissed without prejudice.
  • You have three years from when the infringing activity took place.
  • The CCB can order a party who acted in bad faith to pay costs and fees, up to $5,000, or $2,500 for a party without a lawyer.

The fee table shows $40 when you file and $60 more only if the respondent does not opt out by the end of the opt-out period. If every respondent opts out, you do not pay the second fee. An expedited registration for the CCB route costs $50 per work.

sections.h: The catch: the other side can opt out
sections.html:
The person you name can choose to opt out, and the case then does not proceed at the CCB. Your other option is federal court, where a lawyer is practical. Weigh that before you pay for registration.

This page is general information, not legal advice. For your own case, talk to a copyright lawyer.

q: How to register a copyright in the US
title: How to register a copyright in the US
description: Register art, photos, music or video at the US Copyright Office for $45 to $65 online. Why timing matters and what it lets you claim.
short: Register at the US Copyright Office online. One work by one author costs $45, a standard application $65. Your work is protected from the moment you create it, but registering is required to sue over a US work and decides whether statutory damages and fees are available. Fees change on January 5, 2027.

sections.h: Protected already, registered for the courtroom
sections.html: The Copyright Office says work is under copyright protection the moment it is created and fixed in a tangible form, and that registration is generally voluntary. But you will have to register to bring a lawsuit over a US work, and registered works may be eligible for statutory damages and attorney's fees.

• $45: electronic filing, one author, one work, not made for hire.
  • $65: standard electronic application.
  • $55: group of published or unpublished photographs.
  • $85: group of unpublished works.
  • $125: paper forms.

The office says its fees change on January 5, 2027, so check the current table before you file.

Register within three months of first publishing a work, or before anyone copies it. Past that, copying that began before your registration cannot get statutory damages or attorney's fees (17 U.S.C. 412). Photographers and artists who post often can use a group option to keep this cheap.

1. Create an account on the US Copyright Office's registration site.
  2. Pick the right type of work and whether it is published.
  3. Fill in the author, year and any earlier versions.
  4. Upload a copy of the work and pay the fee.
  5. Keep the confirmation. The office says processing times are on a separate page and change by period.

Mailing a copy to yourself is not a substitute for registration. The Copyright Office says copyright law has no provision for it.

This page is general information, not legal advice. For your own case, talk to a copyright lawyer.

q: Copyright cease and desist letter template
title: Copyright cease and desist letter template
description: A plain cease and desist letter for copied work: what to include, a fill-in template and how it differs from a DMCA takedown.
short: A copyright cease and desist letter tells the person who copied your work what they used, asks them to stop and remove it by a date, and may ask for payment. It has no legal force by itself. A DMCA takedown goes to the platform instead. Use the template below and keep a copy.

sections.html:
• Who you are and that you own the work, with a link to your original and its first publication date.
  • Exactly where the copy is, with links and screenshots.
  • What you want: remove it, stop using it, credit or pay a license fee.
  • A date to respond, such as 10 days.
  • A line saying you reserve your rights.

Keep it calm and factual. Do not threaten anything you will not do.

[Date]

To [name or business]:

I am the creator and copyright owner of [title and description of your work], first published on [date] at [link to original].

I found my work being used without my permission at: [link 1], [link 2]. I have not licensed this use to you.

I ask that you (1) remove the work from every place you posted or sold it, (2) stop using it, and (3) [pay a license fee of $___ / confirm in writing that you have done so] by [date].

This letter does not waive any of my rights or remedies.

[Full name, email, phone]

A cease and desist is a letter to the person. A DMCA takedown notice is sent to the platform or host under a specific law and can get content removed without the copier doing anything. Many creators send the takedown first and a letter only when money is involved.

sections.h: When a letter is not enough

If they ignore it or the copier made money, a lawyer's letter carries more weight, and registered work can support statutory damages of $750 to $30,000 per work (how they work). A lawyer can also tell you whether the copier has a fair use argument.

faqs.a: Run a reverse image search with Google Lens and TinEye, then search its caption or watermark text. If you find a copy you did not license, save proof and report it.

faqs.q: Is reverse image search free?
faqs.a: Google's image search is free. TinEye's site says what it offers; confirm its current limits on tineye.com.

faqs.q: Why does my search find nothing?
faqs.a: A new or private copy may not be indexed, and edited or cropped copies can slip past a simple search. Empty is not proof of absence.

faqs.q: Can I set up alerts?
faqs.a: Some search tools offer alerts. Emera Protect's Creator and Pro plans check your posts on a schedule.

sources.label: Google Search Help: search with an image

cta.p: Creator watches your posts every week and files the takedowns. Start with a free report on a copy you already found.
